sections.title: Complete IC-38 Syllabus - All In One

cards.title: Summary & Q&A
cards.content:
• Origin: Modern insurance started at Lloyd's Coffee House in London.

• HLV Concept: Human Life Value (HLV) calculates the present value of future earnings; introduced by Prof. S.S. Huebner.

• Core Concept: It is a risk transfer mechanism sharing the financial loss of a few among many.

• Insurance vs Assurance: Insurance is for uncertain events (fire/theft); Assurance is for certain events (death).



🎯 HIGHLY REPEATED EXAM Q&A:

Q: Who invented the concept of Human Life Value (HLV)?

A: Prof. S.S. Huebner.

Q: What is the primary function of insurance?

A: To transfer risk and share financial losses.

Q: Where did modern commercial insurance originate?

A: Lloyd's Coffee House, London.

Q: Which term is typically used for Life Insurance contracts?

A: Assurance.

cards.title: Summary & Q&A
cards.content:
• Peril vs Hazard: Peril is the exact cause of loss (e.g., fire). Hazard is a condition that increases the risk of loss.

• Moral Hazard: Intentional dishonesty or fraud (e.g., hiding a medical condition to get insurance).

• Morale Hazard: Carelessness because of having insurance (e.g., leaving a car unlocked).

• Law of Large Numbers: Insurance requires a large pool of people to accurately predict and manage risks.



🎯 HIGHLY REPEATED EXAM Q&A:

Q: A person drives recklessly because he has car insurance. What type of hazard is this?

A: Morale Hazard.

Q: What is the actual event that causes a loss called?

A: Peril.

Q: Hiding a pre-existing heart condition while buying insurance is an example of?

A: Moral Hazard.

Q: Insurance works on the mathematical principle of?

A: Law of Large Numbers.

cards.title: Summary & Q&A
cards.content:
• Utmost Good Faith (Uberrimae Fides): Absolute duty of both parties to disclose all material facts. Hiding facts leads to policy cancellation.

• Insurable Interest: You must suffer a financial loss if the insured dies/gets damaged. In Life Insurance, it MUST exist at the start of the policy.

• Indemnity: Making good the loss. Crucial Exception: Indemnity does NOT apply to Life Insurance (human life has no exact monetary value).

• Subrogation & Contribution: These principles also do NOT apply to Life Insurance.



🎯 HIGHLY REPEATED EXAM Q&A:

Q: Which insurance principle does NOT apply to Life Insurance?

A: Principle of Indemnity.

Q: When must 'Insurable Interest' exist in a Life Insurance contract?

A: Only at the inception (start) of the policy.

Q: What is the legal term for 'Utmost Good Faith'?

A: Uberrimae Fides.

Q: A husband taking a policy on his wife is based on which principle?

A: Insurable Interest.

cards.title: Summary & Q&A
cards.content:
• Indian Contract Act, 1872: Governs all life insurance contracts in India.

• Offer & Acceptance: The customer (proposer) makes the offer. The insurance company accepts it.

• Consideration: The premium paid by the customer is the 'Consideration'.

• Capacity to Contract: Minors (under 18) and persons of unsound mind cannot legally sign an insurance contract.

• Free Consent: Contract is voidable if signed under pressure, fraud, or misrepresentation.



🎯 HIGHLY REPEATED EXAM Q&A:

Q: In an insurance contract, what represents 'Consideration'?

A: The premium paid by the policyholder.

Q: Who makes the 'Offer' in an insurance transaction?

A: The Proposer (Customer).

Q: Which age group is NOT legally competent to enter into an insurance contract?

A: Minors (Below 18 years).

Q: If an agent forces a customer to buy a policy, which contract element is violated?

A: Free Consent.

cards.title: Summary & Q&A
cards.content:
• Underwriting: The process of assessing risk and deciding the premium to be charged.

• Standard Risk: Normal health, charged standard regular premium.

• Sub-standard Risk: Higher risk (bad health, risky job). Accepted but charged an EXTRA premium (called Loading).

• Declined Risk: Unacceptably high risk, proposal is rejected.

• Key Factors: Age is the most critical factor affecting life insurance premiums.



🎯 HIGHLY REPEATED EXAM Q&A:

Q: What action does an insurer take for a 'Sub-standard' risk?

A: Accepts the risk but charges an extra premium (Loading).

Q: What is the primary role of an underwriter?

A: To assess the risk and determine the appropriate premium.

Q: A person with a severe pre-existing disease applies for life insurance. They are likely a?

A: Declined Risk or Sub-standard Risk.

Q: What is the extra premium charged for risky occupations called?

A: Occupational Loading.

cards.title: Summary & Q&A
cards.content:
• Claim Trigger: Occurs upon death, maturity, or surrender.

• TAT (Turnaround Time): Death claims must be settled within 30 days of receiving all necessary documents.

• Disputed Claims: If investigated, investigation must finish within 90 days.

• Penalty for Delay: If the insurer delays payment beyond the deadline, they must pay interest at 2% above the prevailing bank rate.



🎯 HIGHLY REPEATED EXAM Q&A:

Q: What is the standard time limit for an insurer to settle a claim after receiving all documents?

A: 30 days.

Q: What penalty applies if an insurer delays claim settlement?

A: Penal interest at 2% above the bank rate.

Q: If a claim requires investigation, what is the maximum time allowed to complete it?

A: 90 days.

Q: Who initiates a death claim process?

A: The Nominee or Legal Heir.

cards.title: Summary & Q&A
cards.content:
• Proposal Form: The primary base document where the customer declares all details.

• First Premium Receipt (FPR): The ultimate proof that the insurance contract has officially commenced.

• Policy Document: The final legally binding contract detailing all terms and conditions.

• Endorsement: Any written change or correction made to the policy document.



🎯 HIGHLY REPEATED EXAM Q&A:

Q: Which document is the primary basis of the insurance contract?

A: Proposal Form.

Q: Which document serves as absolute proof that the risk has started and the contract is active?

A: First Premium Receipt (FPR).

Q: If a customer changes their address, how is it updated in the policy?

A: Through an Endorsement.

Q: What receipt is issued for subsequent premium payments?

A: Renewal Premium Receipt (RPR).

cards.title: Summary & Q&A
cards.content:
• Intangibility: Insurance cannot be seen or touched; it is a promise. Hence, service trust is essential.

• Point of Sale & Claim: The agent's real test of service is during the claim settlement process.

• CLV (Customer Lifetime Value): The total revenue a customer generates for the insurer over their lifetime.

• Grievances: Poor service leads to low persistency (customers stop paying renewal premiums).



🎯 HIGHLY REPEATED EXAM Q&A:

Q: Insurance is an 'Intangible' product. What does this mean?

A: It is a promise to pay upon a future event; it cannot be physically touched.

Q: What is the most crucial time when an agent must provide high-quality service?

A: At the time of claim settlement.

Q: What is the term for the total economic value a customer brings over their entire relationship with the insurer?

A: Customer Lifetime Value (CLV).

Q: Good customer service directly improves which vital insurance metric?

A: Persistency Rate.

cards.title: Summary & Q&A
cards.content:
• Insurer's Timeline: Insurers must resolve written complaints within 15 days.

• Insurance Ombudsman: A free, out-of-court body for policyholders. NO lawyer is required. NO fee is charged.

• Maximum Award: The Ombudsman can award compensation up to a maximum of ₹30 Lakhs.

• Time Limit to Approach: The complaint must be filed within 1 year of the insurer rejecting the claim.



🎯 HIGHLY REPEATED EXAM Q&A:

Q: What is the maximum claim amount that the Insurance Ombudsman can handle?

A: ₹30 Lakhs.

Q: What is the fee to file a complaint with the Insurance Ombudsman?

A: No fee is required.

Q: Within how many days must an insurance company resolve a customer grievance?

A: 15 days.

Q: What is the time limit to approach the Ombudsman after claim rejection?

A: 1 year.

sections.title: Chapter 10: Regulatory Aspects for Insurance Agents

cards.title: Summary & Q&A
cards.content:
• IRDAI Act 1999: Set up IRDAI to protect policyholders and regulate insurers/agents.

• Section 41 (Rebating): Strictly PROHIBITS agents from sharing their commission or offering discounts to customers to force a sale.

• Agency License: Granted by IRDAI. An agent can only represent ONE life insurance company at a time.

• Code of Conduct: Agents must display their ID, explain terms transparently, and not hide exclusions.



🎯 HIGHLY REPEATED EXAM Q&A:

Q: Which section of the Insurance Act strictly prohibits agents from offering rebates or sharing commissions?

A: Section 41.

Q: Can an agent sell life insurance policies for LIC and HDFC Life at the same time?

A: No, an agent can represent only one Life Insurance company.

Q: Who issues the license to insurance agents in India?

A: IRDAI.

Q: What is the basic educational qualification required to become an insurance agent?

A: Pass 10th standard (or equivalent).

cards.title: Summary & Q&A
cards.content:
• Two Primary Risks: "Dying too early" (loss of income for dependents) and "Living too long" (outliving savings).

• Protection + Savings: Traditional life insurance offers a death cover and builds a cash value over time.

• Pure Term: Only provides death protection, no cash/savings value.

• Asset Protection: Life insurance replaces the lost Human Life Value (HLV).



🎯 HIGHLY REPEATED EXAM Q&A:

Q: What are the two fundamental risks addressed by Life Insurance?

A: Dying too early and living too long.

Q: Which type of life insurance policy has NO savings or cash value component?

A: Pure Term Insurance.

Q: Life insurance aims to replace the loss of what economic concept?

A: Human Life Value (HLV).

Q: How does life insurance manage financial risk?

A: By pooling the risks of many people.

cards.title: Summary & Q&A
cards.content:
• Inflation: The biggest enemy of long-term planning, as it reduces the purchasing power of money.

• Emergency Fund: The very first step in financial planning is keeping 3-6 months of expenses in a liquid bank account.

• Life Stages: Accumulation (20-40 years), Conservation (40-60 years), Distribution (60+ years / Retirement).

• Goal Setting: Planning must match specific time-bound life goals (child education, retirement).



🎯 HIGHLY REPEATED EXAM Q&A:

Q: What is the primary factor that decreases the future purchasing power of money?

A: Inflation.

Q: In the financial life cycle, the 'Distribution Phase' typically refers to which period?

A: Post-retirement (Age 60+).

Q: What should be the first step in an individual's financial planning journey?

A: Creating an Emergency Fund.

Q: What is the primary objective of financial planning?

A: To achieve life goals systematically.

cards.title: Summary & Q&A
cards.content:
• Term Insurance: Pure death benefit. Lowest premium, highest cover. Nothing is paid if the person survives.

• Endowment Policy: Pays out on death OR maturity (whichever is earlier). Has a savings component.

• Whole Life Policy: Covers a person for their entire life (up to 99/100 years). Best for leaving an estate for heirs.

• Money Back Policy: Pays a percentage of the Sum Assured at regular intervals as survival benefits.



🎯 HIGHLY REPEATED EXAM Q&A:

Q: Which life insurance product offers the maximum death cover at the lowest premium?

A: Term Insurance.

Q: Which policy pays periodic survival benefits during the term of the policy?

A: Money Back Policy.

Q: Which policy is best suited for leaving a legacy or estate for one's children?

A: Whole Life Policy.

Q: An Endowment policy provides benefits on?

A: Death or Maturity, whichever occurs first.

cards.title: Summary & Q&A
cards.content:
• ULIP (Unit Linked Insurance Plan): Combines life cover with market-linked investments (Mutual Fund style).

• Investment Risk: The risk is entirely borne by the POLICYHOLDER, not the insurance company.

• Transparency: All charges (mortality, fund management) are clearly unbundled and disclosed.

• Lock-in Period: Strict 5-year mandatory lock-in period for all ULIPs before withdrawal.

• NAV: Net Asset Value determines the daily price of the ULIP units.



🎯 HIGHLY REPEATED EXAM Q&A:

Q: In a ULIP, who bears the investment risk of the stock market?

A: The Policyholder.

Q: What is the mandatory lock-in period for a Unit Linked Insurance Plan (ULIP)?

A: 5 Years.

Q: The value of units in a ULIP is determined by what metric?

A: Net Asset Value (NAV).

Q: What feature allows a ULIP policyholder to move money between equity and debt funds?

A: Fund Switching.

cards.title: Summary & Q&A
cards.content:
• MWP Act (Section 6): Married Women's Property Act creates a trust. Death benefit is legally protected from creditors/courts.

• MWP Beneficiaries: ONLY the wife, or children, or both can be beneficiaries.

• Keyman Insurance: Bought by a company on the life of its most crucial employee. Premium is a business expense.

• Keyman Claim: Death benefit is paid to the EMPLOYER (company), and it is fully taxable.



🎯 HIGHLY REPEATED EXAM Q&A:

Q: Who can be made beneficiaries under a policy endorsed under the MWP Act?

A: Wife and/or Children only.

Q: A policy issued under the MWP Act is protected from whom?

A: Creditors and Court Attachments.

Q: In Keyman Insurance, who receives the claim money if the Keyman dies?

A: The Employer (The Company).

Q: Can the Keyman's family claim the death benefit in Keyman Insurance?

A: No, only the company can claim it.

sections.title: Chapter 16: Pricing and Valuation in Life Insurance

cards.title: Summary & Q&A
cards.content:
• Premium Formula: Premium = Mortality Cost + Expenses - Interest.

• Mortality Cost: Cost of covering the death risk. It goes UP as age increases.

• Interest Earned: Insurers invest premiums. Higher interest earned means LOWER premiums for customers.

• Actuarial Valuation: Calculating assets vs liabilities to determine the company's surplus/profits.

• Bonus: Reversionary bonuses are declared out of this surplus for 'Participating' policyholders.



🎯 HIGHLY REPEATED EXAM Q&A:

Q: What are the three basic elements used to calculate life insurance premiums?

A: Mortality, Expenses, and Interest.

Q: As the age of the proposer increases, what happens to the mortality cost?

A: It increases.

Q: What is the purpose of conducting an Actuarial Valuation?

A: To assess the insurer's liabilities and determine surplus (profit) for bonus distribution.

Q: Which component REDUCES the final premium charged to the customer?

A: Expected Interest Earnings.

cards.title: Summary & Q&A
cards.content:
• Standard Age Proof: Highly reliable (Passport, PAN Card, 10th Certificate).

• Non-Standard Age Proof: Less reliable (Horoscope, Village Panchayat cert). Requires extra premium loading.

• Nomination (Section 39): Appointing someone to receive the death benefit. Nominee is just a trustee, not owner.

• Assignment (Section 38): Transferring total ownership rights of the policy to someone else (e.g., to a bank for a loan).

• Free Look Period: 15 days to return the policy and get a refund if the customer doesn't like the terms.



🎯 HIGHLY REPEATED EXAM Q&A:

Q: Under which section of the Insurance Act is 'Nomination' made?

A: Section 39.

Q: A policy is pledged to a bank to take a loan. What is this process called?

A: Assignment (Section 38).

Q: What is the 'Free Look Period' for a life insurance policy bought through an agent?

A: 15 Days.

Q: Which of the following is considered a 'Standard Age Proof'?

A: Passport / PAN Card.

cards.title: Summary & Q&A
cards.content:
• Non-Medical Underwriting: Approving policies without medical tests (based purely on form details and young age).

• Financial Underwriting: Checking income proofs to ensure the person is not buying excessive coverage (prevents moral hazard).

• Numerical Rating Method: A system where positive/negative points are given to health factors to calculate the final risk score.

• Occupation Loading: High-risk jobs (Pilots, Miners) are charged higher premiums.



🎯 HIGHLY REPEATED EXAM Q&A:

Q: What is the main purpose of Financial Underwriting?

A: To ensure the Sum Assured matches the person's income and prevent moral hazard.

Q: Which underwriting method assigns mathematical points to various health and risk factors?

A: Numerical Rating Method.

Q: Issuing a policy strictly based on the proposal form without blood/urine tests is called?

A: Non-Medical Underwriting.

Q: Why is female underwriting sometimes treated differently?

A: Due to pregnancy and maternity-related complications.

cards.title: Summary & Q&A
cards.content:
• Early Claim: Death happening within 3 years of policy start. Highly investigated for fraud/hiding facts.

• Section 45 (Indisputability): NO policy can be rejected or questioned on ANY grounds after 3 years.

• Grace Period: Extra time to pay premium. 30 days for Yearly/Half-yearly modes. 15 days for Monthly mode.

• Lapsed Policy: If premium is unpaid after the grace period, the policy lapses. It can be 'revived' later.



🎯 HIGHLY REPEATED EXAM Q&A:

Q: According to Section 45, an insurer cannot reject a claim on any grounds after how many years?

A: 3 Years.

Q: A death occurring within 3 years of taking the policy is classified as?

A: Early Claim.

Q: What is the standard grace period for a monthly premium payment mode?

A: 15 Days.

Q: If a policyholder dies during the grace period, will the claim be paid?

A: Yes, the claim is paid after deducting the unpaid premium.

cards.title: Summary & Q&A
cards.content:
• Purpose: To protect savings against sudden, high hospitalization and medical bills.

• Medical Inflation: Healthcare costs are rising rapidly, much faster than general inflation.

• Morbidity Risk: Health insurance deals with 'Morbidity' (risk of falling sick). Life insurance deals with 'Mortality' (death).

• Out-of-Pocket Expense: In India, a major portion of healthcare is still paid directly from the patient's pocket, proving the need for insurance.



🎯 HIGHLY REPEATED EXAM Q&A:

Q: Health insurance primarily assesses which type of risk?

A: Morbidity Risk (Incidence of sickness/disease).

Q: What is the main driver making health insurance essential today?

A: High Medical Inflation.

Q: The risk of death is called mortality. What is the risk of disease or disability called?

A: Morbidity.

Q: What is it called when a patient pays for treatment from their own savings?

A: Out-of-pocket expenses.

cards.title: Summary & Q&A
cards.content:
• TPA (Third Party Administrator): Intermediary agency that processes cashless claims and manages the hospital network.

• Health Card: Issued by TPA. Essential to carry to the hospital for cashless treatment.

• Pre-Policy Checkup: Medical tests required for older applicants (usually 45+) before giving health insurance.

• Portability: Transferring your health policy to a new company WITHOUT losing the waiting period benefits already served.



🎯 HIGHLY REPEATED EXAM Q&A:

Q: Who acts as the intermediary between the insurer, hospital, and customer for cashless claims?

A: Third Party Administrator (TPA).

Q: What is the mechanism that allows you to switch health insurance companies without losing waiting period benefits?

A: Portability.

Q: Which document must be shown at the hospital admission desk to avail cashless treatment?

A: Health Card.

Q: At what age do most insurers typically demand a mandatory pre-policy medical checkup?

A: Usually above 45 or 50 years.

cards.title: Summary & Q&A
cards.content:
• Indemnity (Mediclaim): Pays exact hospital bills. If bill is 1 Lakh, it pays 1 Lakh.

• Fixed Benefit (Critical Illness): Pays a massive lump sum (e.g., 10 Lakhs) instantly upon diagnosis of cancer/heart attack, regardless of bill size.

• Family Floater: One policy, one single Sum Insured covering husband, wife, and kids. Anyone can use the pool.

• Day Care Procedures: Surgeries taking less than 24 hours (like Cataract) due to modern technology.



🎯 HIGHLY REPEATED EXAM Q&A:

Q: Which health policy pays a lump sum amount upon the diagnosis of a specified major disease?

A: Critical Illness Policy.

Q: A single health policy covering the entire family under one overall sum insured is called?

A: Family Floater Policy.

Q: A cataract surgery that requires discharge on the same day is classified as?

A: Day Care Procedure.

Q: A basic Mediclaim policy operates on which principle?

A: Principle of Indemnity.

cards.title: Summary & Q&A
cards.content:
• PED (Pre-Existing Disease): Any disease diagnosed or treated within 48 months before buying the policy.

• Maximum Waiting Period: Standard PED waiting period is 4 years (48 months).

• Co-payment Clause: The customer agrees to pay a fixed percentage (e.g., 10%) of every claim bill from their own pocket.

• Deductible: A fixed initial amount the customer must pay before the insurance starts paying.



🎯 HIGHLY REPEATED EXAM Q&A:

Q: What is the maximum permitted waiting period for Pre-Existing Diseases (PED) in standard health policies?

A: 48 Months (4 years).

Q: A clause where the policyholder must pay a specific percentage of the total claim amount is called?

A: Co-payment.

Q: What is the standard initial waiting period during which no sickness claims are paid (except accidents)?

A: 30 Days.

Q: A pre-existing disease is a condition diagnosed within how many months before policy inception?

A: 48 Months.

cards.title: Summary & Q&A
cards.content:
• Cashless Claim: The insurance company pays the hospital directly. Must be done at a 'Network Hospital'.

• Reimbursement Claim: Customer pays first, then submits bills to insurer for a refund. Can be done at Non-Network hospitals.

• Permanent Exclusions: Things NEVER paid by health insurance (Cosmetic surgery, self-inflicted injury, unprescribed vitamins).

• Claim Intimation: Must usually inform TPA within 24 hours of an emergency admission.



🎯 HIGHLY REPEATED EXAM Q&A:

Q: To avail a cashless claim facility, where must the patient be admitted?

A: A Network Hospital.

Q: Are cosmetic surgeries and self-inflicted injuries covered under standard health policies?

A: No, they are permanent exclusions.

Q: What is the process called when a patient pays the bill first and claims the money back from the insurer later?

A: Reimbursement Claim.

Q: For planned hospitalization, when should the TPA generally be informed?

A: 48 to 72 hours prior to admission.
